nameStory: The Garden Lithobius gets its name from its habit of lurking in garden soil and compost piles, where gardeners often encounter it while digging. 'Lithobius' comes from Greek words meaning 'stone life,' referring to how these centipedes love hiding under rocks and in rocky crevices.
description: The Garden Lithobius is a fast-moving centipede with a flattened, reddish-brown body that's perfectly built for squeezing through tight spaces in soil and leaf litter. Like all centipedes, it has one pair of legs per body segment (unlike millipedes which have two pairs), giving it 15 pairs of legs total. This cosmopolitan species grows to about 1-1.5 inches long and is one of the most widespread centipedes in the world. Despite its fearsome appearance, it's actually beneficial to gardeners since it hunts pest insects.

idTips.label: Body segments and legs
idTips.description: Count 15 pairs of legs - one pair per body segment. The legs get progressively longer toward the back, with the last pair extending well beyond the body like trailing antennae.

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Look for a reddish-brown to golden-brown body with darker stripes running lengthwise. The head is typically darker than the body segments.

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Moves in characteristic quick, undulating bursts when disturbed, then freezes motionless. The motion looks almost snake-like as it flows over obstacles.

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Feels firm and slightly waxy to the touch, with a distinctly flattened profile that lets it slip easily under your finger when handled.

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: About as long as your thumb (1-1.5 inches) but much narrower, with a head that's noticeably wider than the body segments behind it.

habitat: Look for Garden Lithobius in moist soil around gardens, compost piles, and under logs or stones in wooded areas throughout New England. They prefer areas with rich organic matter where they can hunt for small insects and stay hidden during the day. You'll often find them in basement window wells, under mulch, or in the leaf litter layer of deciduous forests.

seasonality.spring: Becomes active as soil warms, often found when turning garden soil or moving stones. This is prime time for spotting them as they emerge from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Most active during warm nights, hiding under objects during hot days. Look for them under watering cans, flower pots, or in compost bins where moisture levels stay high.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move deeper into soil and under larger objects for winter protection. Often discovered during fall garden cleanup activities.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep in soil, under foundations, or in protected spaces like basements. Rarely seen unless you're digging in protected, unfrozen soil.

funFact: Garden Lithobius can detach their own legs when grabbed by a predator - the detached leg keeps twitching for several minutes to distract the attacker while the centipede escapes, and it can regenerate the lost leg over several molts!
confusionNotes: Often confused with millipedes, but remember: centipedes are fast and have one pair of legs per segment, while millipedes are slow and have two pairs per segment. Memory trick: 'CENTipede = one pair per segment, MILLIpede = Multiple pairs per segment.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'European steppe centipede,' this species is now found worldwide and is actually beneficial in gardens - it's a natural pest controller that hunts insects, slugs, and other garden pests. Many people fear centipedes unnecessarily when they're actually garden allies.
compareHints: Garden Lithobius is distinguished from the Brown Centipede by its reddish-brown coloration and slightly smaller size, while the Least Lithobius is much smaller overall. The Garden Lithobius also tends to be more commonly found in cultivated areas like gardens and compost piles, whereas its relatives prefer wilder forest habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Brown Centipede is larger and more robust than its relatives the Garden Lithobius and Least Lithobius.
The Least Lithobius is significantly smaller and more delicate than its relatives the Brown Centipede and Garden Lithobius, which can grow much larger and have more robust builds.
